title: Sandpiper
wiki_lead:
Scolopacidae is a large family of shorebirds, or waders, which mainly includes many species known as sandpipers, but also others such as woodcocks, curlews, and snipes. Most of these species eat small invertebrates picked out of the mud or soil. There is no evidence that different lengths of bills enable multiple species to feed in the same habitat, particularly on the coast, without direct competition for food. On sandy beaches, species with different bill lengths feed on the only abundant invertebrate, such as mole crabs Emerita.
Sandpipers have long bodies and legs, and narrow wings. Most species have a narrow bill, but the form and length are variable. They are small to medium-sized birds, measuring 12 to 66 cm (4.7–26.0 in) in length. The bills are sensitive, allowing the birds to feel the mud and sand as they probe for food. They generally have dull plumage, with cryptic brown, grey, or streaked patterns, although some display brighter colours during the breeding season.
Most species nest in open areas and defend their territories with aerial displays. The nest itself is a simple scrape in the ground, in which the bird typically lays three or four eggs. The young of most species are precocial.

Taxonomy
The family Scolopacidae was introduced (as Scolopacea) by the French polymath Constantine Samuel Rafinesque in 1815. The family contains 98 extant or recently extinct species divided into 15 genera. For more details, see the article List of sandpiper species.
The following genus-level cladogram of the Scolopacidae is based on a study by David Černý and Rossy Natale that was published in 2022.


Fossil record
The early fossil record of Scolopacidae is relatively fragmentary, with several Paleogene specimens of uncertain taxonomic placement. Among the oldest reported members is the extinct Paractitis bardi, known from a partial coracoid recovered from the Cypress Hills Formation of Saskatchewan, Canada. Originally considered Early Oligocene in age, the fossil has subsequently been assigned to the Late Eocene. Its placement within Scolopacidae remains uncertain, particularly because the preserved coracoid lacks the supracoracoideus nerve foramen characteristic of Scolopaci. An almost complete postcranial skeleton from the Early Oligocene of the Luberon region in southern France has also been referred to Scolopacidae, although its precise relationships within the family remain unresolved.
More extensive remains are known from the Early Miocene lacustrine deposits of Saint-Gérand-le-Puy, Allier, in central France. The assemblage includes the extinct scolopacids Elorius paludicola and Parvelorius gracilis, the latter originally assigned to the living genus Tringa. Two additional species, Elorius limosoides and Parvelorius calidris, are tentatively referred to these extinct genera. Their remains include elements of the skull, humerus, coracoid and tarsometatarsus, with anatomical features distinguishing them from living scolopacids. The same deposits have yielded Scolopacimilis lartetianus, originally described as Totanus lartetianus, and Becassius charadriioides. Both exhibit a combination of skeletal characteristics differing from those of extant Scolopacidae, and their inclusion within the family remains uncertain.
The Middle Miocene deposits of the Nördlinger Ries basin in Bavaria, Germany, have yielded the extinct genus Mirolia, represented by M. brevirostrata, M. dubia, M. parvula and the tentatively assigned M. mascalidris. The fossils comprise cranial and postcranial elements, including the mandible, humerus, coracoid and tarsometatarsus. Their morphology indicates affinities with Calidridinae, particularly in the proportions of the bill and several features of the humerus. Mirolia brevirostrata is among the oldest fossil representatives used to establish the minimum evolutionary age of the calidrid lineage.
Other Miocene scolopacids include Numenius antiquus from Sansan in France, known from fragments of the tarsometat
grok_lead: Sandpipers comprise the family Scolopacidae, a diverse group of approximately 97 species of shorebirds within the order Charadriiformes, known for their slender builds, long legs, and bills adapted for probing soft substrates in search of invertebrates. These waders range in size from small peeps like the least sandpiper (about 13â15 cm long) to larger curlews exceeding 60 cm, with plumage typically in cryptic browns and grays for camouflage, though some display vibrant breeding colors. The family encompasses subgroups such as true sandpipers ( Calidris), curlews (Numenius), godwits (Limosa), snipes ( Gallinago), woodcocks (Scolopax), and phalaropes (Phalaropus), each with specialized foraging and locomotion traits. Scolopacids exhibit a nearly global distribution, occurring across all continents except Antarctica and the most arid deserts, with the majority breeding in northern temperate to Arctic regions. Preferred breeding habitats include wet, open areas such as tundra, marshes, bogs, grasslands, and forest edges, where they nest in shallow scrapes on the ground. Many species are highly migratory, traveling thousands of kilometers from high-latitude nesting grounds to winter in tropical coastal mudflats, estuaries, lakeshores, and inland wetlands, often forming large flocks during migration and non-breeding seasons. These birds primarily feed on insects, crustaceans, mollusks, and worms detected by touch-sensitive bill tips, employing techniques like stitching (rapid pecking) or deeper probing depending on bill morphology. Notable behaviors include polyandry in phalaropes, where females are more colorful and competitive while males incubate eggs, and elaborate aerial displays in woodcocks. While most species remain common, some face threats from habitat degradation, hunting, and climate-driven changes to breeding and stopover sites, highlighting the importance of wetland conservation.
